newsitem.title: UK: Italy to benefit from Spanish rate cut.
newsitem.headline: Italy to benefit from Spanish rate cut.

text.p: International investor attention will focus once more on Italy after the Bank of Spain met market expectations and cut interest rates on Tuesday, analysts said.
"The Bank of Spain has managed the process of getting interest rates down very effectively," said Ifty Islam, European bond strategist at Merrill Lynch in London.
"The Bank of Italy's approach on interest rates is a little bit more surprising."
The Bank of Spain earlier cut its key money rate to 5.50 percent from 5.75 percent at its regular repurchase tender.
The rate move was widely anticipated and market reaction was muted. The Spanish 10-year June bond future was trading at 113.64 at 0947 GMT, 21 basis points above Monday's close.
"Spain has been outperforming Italy," said David Brown, chief international economist at Bear Stearns in London.
"There has been a very strong determination to hedge your high yield bets by being overweight Spain, but Italy will make a comeback short term."
The Bank of Italy has been tipped to cut interest rates for some weeks.
"A lot of people have had that trade on for a long time and been disappointed by it," said Islam.
Low inflation in March is likely to develop into sub-two percent Italian inflation in the second quarter, economists said.
But political turmoil in Prime Minister Romano Prodi's government over the sending of a security force to Albania has held Italy's central bank back, they added.
The Spanish economy still compares favourably with Italy, analysts said.

"There is a strong conviction that Spain will be part of a first round of monetary union, and the fundamentals are sufficiently positive to justify that," said Eric Fishwick, international economist at Nikko Europe in London.
"But Spain is trading 60 basis points through gilt yields, and the risk is that the peripherals do come under pressure towards the end of the year," he added.
Question marks over the timetable for European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) will affect spreads in all the high-yielding bond markets, economists said.
The 10-year Bonos/Bund spread can narrow from its current 95 basis points to 80 basis points, but will widen to 125 basis points on a one to two month basis, Brown said.
The BTP/Bund spread will move in to 150 basis points from 167 basis points currently, but will stretch above 200 basis points longer term, he added.
But there is room for the markets to swing back in Italy's favour, economists said.
"The idea that Italy will be excluded altogether from EMU while Spain is in, is not feasible even if Italy's entry is delayed by a year," said Islam.
"The credit spread between the two countries after EMU will not be more than 20-25 basis points, so the yield spread between Italy and Spain will narrow before then," he added.
Portugal and Sweden also look attractive higher-yielding alternatives, analysts said.
"Portugal is one of the hidden stars," said Fishwick.
"Its fundamentals are very, very strong, and there is quite a respectable chance that Portugal can be part of the first round of EMU."
The Bank of Portugal cut interest rates on Friday.
"But it has a small bond market where at times liquidity becomes questionable," Fishwick added.
Sweden releases its budget at 1100 GMT, but the details of an expansionary budget to be financed by a projected budget surplus in 1998 were leaked to the press in advance.
"It is difficult to argue that a budget surplus in 1998 is bad news," said Islam.
